Haha, yeah, it's a bit difficult. The trickiest part is the apostrophes that separate words in compounds. They make different vowel sounds, depending on the sounds next to them.

Here's a more or less complete list of the sounds that correspond to the letters:

Vowels IPA
a a
e ɛ
i ɪ
u ʌ
Consonants IPA
b b
c ç
d d
f f
g g
h h
j ʒ
k k
l l
p p
r ɾ
s s
t t
v v
x x
y j
z z
þ θ
ð ð
ß ʃ
' ʔ
Digraphs IPA
be m
de n
ge ŋ
rr r
yu w
Digraphs IPA
au o
uu u
ei e
ii i

To split up the digraphs, you would put a rising diacritic over the last letter of it, which will make each letter be sounded out, individually, such as <aú> /au/. A shining example of this, in a word, would be aúbéíi /aubɛi/, where there are three broken up diacritics: <aú>, <bé>, and <éí>. In <éí>, the <e> having a diacritic on it means nothing, because it has to be on the final letter of the digraph to count. If it were <béi>, without the diacritic on the <i>, it would be pronounced /be/, because of the <éi>. Also, letters that are already in diacritics don't alter letters after it. For instance, if aúbéíi were spelled aúbeii. It would, then, be pronounced as /aumi/.

Also, some apostrophes don't count. Like in " 'dé," which is a shortened version of "dayaude'dé." Apostrophes in this case make no sounds, and they're all over the language in informal speech. Also, if I'm translating it into the southern dialect, apostrophes between words in compounds make no sounds, and all voiced fricatives are unvoiced.
